messages.content:
You check what a company's executives said on an earnings call against the company's annual report (Form 10-K), as a careful analyst would. You get one claim from the call and a few numbered 10-K passages found by search. For each passage, decide how it bears on the claim:

- contradiction: both are about the same thing (the same measure, scope and period, or the same fact about the company) and they can't both be true: figures that differ by more than rounding, opposite directions, or one saying something is so and the other that it isn't.
- consistent: the passage states the same thing, or something that agrees with it.
- unrelated: the passage doesn't speak to what the claim states, or covers a different period, segment or measure.

Not contradictions:
- A forecast, target or plan, and a different actual result for that period or a later, revised target. Plans change; that's news, not a contradiction.
- A risk the 10-K says could happen, and executives sounding confident on the call.
- Figures for different periods or scopes: a quarter and the full year, one segment and the whole company, adjusted (non-GAAP) and reported figures.
- Rounding, different wording, or one side giving more detail.
Flag a contradiction only when an analyst shown the two quotes side by side would agree they can't both be true.

The call quote is what was said; the claim sentence summarizes it to help you read it. The transcript is a machine transcription, so a misspelled name is still the same name.

For each passage, give a short reason first (what each side says), then the verdict, and filing_quote: the clause of the passage the verdict rests on, copied exactly, character for character, at most about 40 words. Leave filing_quote empty when the passage is unrelated.

Company: SITIME Corp

On the Q3 2020 earnings call, Art Chadwick said (metric):
Quote: "gross margins increased 530 basis points from Q2 to Q3"
Claim: SITIME Corp gross margins increased 530 basis points from Q2 to Q3.

10-K passages:

[F1] 10-K for fiscal 2020, filed 2021-02-16 · Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations › Pricing, Product Cost, and Product Mix
Gross margin, or gross profit as a percentage of revenue, has been, and will continue to be, affected by a variety of factors, including ASPs, and product mix in a given period, material costs, yields, inventory write-downs and manufacturing operations costs. We believe the primary driver of gross margin is the ASPs negotiated between us and our customers relative to material costs and yield improvement. As our products mature and unit volumes increase, we expect their ASPs to decline. These declines often coincide with improvements in manufacturing yields and lower wafer, assembly, and testing costs, which offset some or all of the margin reduction that results from lower ASPs. However, we expect our gross margin to fluctuate on a quarterly basis as a result of changes in ASPs due to new product introductions, existing product transitions into high-volume manufacturing, manufacturing costs, and our product mix.

[F2] 10-K for fiscal 2020, filed 2021-02-16 · Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations › Cost of Revenue, Gross Profit, and Gross Margin
Gross margin was higher by 3% in the year ended December 31, 2020 compared to the same period in 2019. The gross margin for the year ended 2019 included a benefit of 3% or $2.5 million from sale of previously reserved inventory. The gross margin excluding the benefit to the gross margin from the sale of the previously reserved inventory increased by 6% year over year from higher sales volume and an increase in ASPs offset in part by higher other manufacturing costs.

[F3] 10-K for fiscal 2020, filed 2021-02-16 · Item 1A. Risk Factors › Our gross margins may fluctuate due to a variety of factors, which could negatively impact our results of operations and our financial condition.
Because we do not operate our own manufacturing, assembly, or testing facilities, we may not be able to reduce our costs as rapidly as companies that operate their own facilities, and our costs may even increase, which could further reduce our gross margins. We rely primarily on obtaining yield improvements and volume-based cost reductions to drive cost reductions in the manufacture of existing products, introducing new products that incorporate advanced features and optimize die size, and other price and performance factors that enable us to increase revenue while maintaining gross margins. To the extent that such cost reductions or revenue increases do not occur at a sufficient level and in a timely manner, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

In addition, we maintain an inventory of our products at various stages of production and in some cases as finished good inventory. We hold these inventories in anticipation of customer orders. If those customer orders do not materialize in a timely manner, we may have excess or obsolete inventory which we would have to reserve or write-down, and our gross margins would be adversely affected.

source.description: Label of the 10-K passage, e.g. F2

reason.description: What each side says, and why that's the verdict

filing_quote.description: Exact text from the passage the verdict rests on; empty if unrelated
